title: Encyclopedia of Chart Patterns, 3rd Edition
author: Thomas N. Bulkowski
summary:
*Encyclopedia of Chart Patterns* is a reference work rather than a narrative book: it catalogs roughly 75 chart patterns — reversal patterns, continuation patterns, candlestick-style short-term patterns, and event-driven patterns — each documented with identification guidelines, statistically-derived performance data, common failure modes, and trading tactics. Thomas Bulkowski built the book from his own multi-decade personal database of tens of thousands of individual pattern occurrences across real stocks, which is what distinguishes it from purely descriptive technical analysis texts: every pattern entry comes with quantified statistics on how often the pattern actually performs as expected, how often it fails, and what specific variations correlate with better or worse outcomes.

Because this is a reference encyclopedia rather than a linear argument, this entry groups its ~75 individual pattern chapters into broader thematic sections for the purposes of whole-book synthesis, rather than summarizing each pattern chapter individually (see Source Notes). The book opens with methodology chapters explaining how Bulkowski defines and measures a pattern, what counts as a "breakout," how he calculates failure rates, and how to read the statistical tables that accompany every pattern — this methodological foundation matters because the same visual pattern can be defined slightly differently by different analysts, which changes the resulting statistics substantially.

The bulk of the book is organized around pattern families: classic reversal patterns like head-and-shoulders, double and triple tops/bottoms, and broadening formations; continuation patterns like flags, pennants, and triangles that suggest a pause within an ongoing trend rather than its end; shorter-term candlestick-adjacent patterns; and "event patterns" driven by specific corporate or macro events (earnings surprises, stock buybacks, dividend announcements) rather than pure price geometry. For each pattern, Bulkowski reports statistics such as average rise or decline after a confirmed breakout, the percentage of patterns that fail to perform as expected, how often price pulls back to "kiss" the breakout level before continuing, and which visual variations of the pattern (such as narrower versus wider formations) correlate with stronger subsequent performance.

The book closes with chapters on trading tactics that apply across patterns generally — money management principles, how to combine multiple confirming signals, and setting realistic expectations given that even the best-performing patterns in Bulkowski's database still fail a meaningful percentage of the time. The overriding message across the entire encyclopedia is empirical humility: chart patterns are probabilistic tools with measurable, imperfect success rates, not guarantees, and Bulkowski's central contribution is replacing folklore-level claims about pattern reliability with actual measured statistics, however unglamorous or pattern-deflating some of those numbers turn out to be.

sections.title: Chart Pattern Methodology and Statistics
sections.summary:
This opening section lays out how Bulkowski defines a pattern for statistical measurement purposes, including precise rules for what counts as a valid instance of a pattern, how breakouts are identified and measured, and how failure is defined and calculated across his sample. This matters because vague, informal pattern definitions are common in trading folklore, and Bulkowski's statistics are only meaningful given consistent, disclosed measurement rules.
The chapters here also explain how to read the recurring statistical tables that accompany every pattern entry later in the book — metrics like average post-breakout move, throwback/pullback frequency, and performance by breakout direction — so that later pattern-specific chapters can be read as reference lookups rather than requiring re-explanation each time.
This section closes by setting reader expectations: even well-defined, well-performing patterns fail a meaningful share of the time in Bulkowski's data, and the goal of measurement is realistic probability assessment, not a search for a guaranteed pattern.
keyLessons: Consistent, disclosed measurement rules are what make pattern statistics meaningful rather than folklore.
Learning to read the recurring statistical tables is necessary to use the rest of the book as a reference.
Even well-performing patterns fail a meaningful percentage of the time; expect probability, not certainty.

sections.title: Reversal Patterns
sections.summary:
This large section covers classic trend-reversal formations such as head-and-shoulders tops and bottoms, double and triple tops and bottoms, broadening tops and bottoms, and rounding patterns — formations that suggest an existing trend is exhausting and about to turn. Each pattern chapter documents identification rules, common variations, and Bulkowski's measured statistics on post-breakout performance and failure rates.
A recurring finding across this section is that supposedly similar-looking reversal patterns can have meaningfully different statistical performance depending on specific measurable details — the depth of a pattern, the volume behavior during formation, or the overall market trend context at the time — which Bulkowski treats as more decision-relevant than the pattern's basic visual shape alone.
The section closes by reinforcing that reversal patterns, despite popular trading folklore treating some (like head-and-shoulders) as near-guarantees, still carry real, quantified failure rates that traders need to plan around rather than assume away.
keyLessons: Visually similar reversal patterns can have meaningfully different real-world performance based on measurable details.
Volume behavior and market trend context often matter as much as the pattern's basic shape.
Even iconic patterns like head-and-shoulders have real, quantified failure rates worth planning around.

sections.title: Continuation Patterns
sections.summary:
This section covers patterns that typically appear as pauses within an ongoing trend rather than reversals of it — flags, pennants, triangles (ascending, descending, symmetrical), rectangles, and related formations. These patterns are generally shorter in duration than major reversal patterns and are traded with the expectation that the prior trend will resume after the pause.
Bulkowski's statistics here focus heavily on how reliably these patterns actually predict trend continuation versus how often they instead mark an unexpected reversal, along with measured data on typical breakout timing and magnitude for each specific pattern shape.
The section closes by noting that continuation patterns, while generally shorter-term and higher-frequency than major reversal patterns, are not simply "safer" by default — Bulkowski's data shows meaningful variation in reliability even within this pattern family depending on the specific formation.
keyLessons: Continuation patterns are traded on the expectation of trend resumption, not as guaranteed continuations.
Reliability varies meaningfully across specific continuation pattern shapes, not uniformly across the whole family.
Breakout timing and magnitude statistics differ pattern by pattern within this category.

sections.title: Candlestick and Short-Term Patterns
sections.summary:
This section addresses shorter-duration, often single- or few-candle formations that traders use for near-term entry and exit timing rather than major trend calls. Bulkowski applies the same statistical rigor here as with longer-term patterns, measuring how often these short-term signals actually precede the price move traders commonly associate with them.
A notable theme in this section is that some widely taught short-term patterns perform meaningfully worse in Bulkowski's measured data than their popular reputation suggests, which he presents plainly rather than softening to match trading folklore.
The section closes by cautioning that shorter-term patterns generally carry more noise and lower statistical reliability than longer-duration formations, making them best used as one input alongside other confirming signals rather than as standalone trade triggers.
keyLessons: Short-term pattern performance should be measured against actual data, not assumed from popular reputation.
Some widely taught short-term patterns underperform their folklore reputation in Bulkowski's measured data.
Short-term patterns are best combined with other confirming signals rather than used as standalone triggers.

sections.title: Event Patterns
sections.summary:
This section covers patterns driven by specific corporate or macro events — earnings surprises, stock buyback announcements, dividend changes, and similar catalysts — rather than by pure price geometry. These patterns are measured similarly to price-based ones, but the underlying cause is an identifiable news event rather than a visually recurring shape.
Bulkowski's data here explores how markets tend to react to different categories of corporate news, including how often an initial post-announcement move tends to continue versus reverse, and what pre- and post-event price behavior tends to look like on average.
The section closes by connecting event patterns back to the book's broader empirical approach: even fundamentally-driven price reactions can be studied with the same statistical rigor as purely technical chart shapes, and doing so often reveals that market reactions to common event types are less uniformly predictable than assumed.
keyLessons: Event patterns are driven by identifiable news catalysts rather than pure chart geometry.
Post-announcement price behavior can be studied statistically the same way technical patterns are.
Market reactions to common corporate events are often less uniformly predictable than commonly assumed.

sections.title: Trading Tactics and Money Management
sections.summary:
The closing section shifts from individual pattern statistics to general principles for trading any pattern responsibly: position sizing, setting stop-losses based on pattern-specific invalidation points, and combining multiple confirming signals rather than trading a single pattern signal in isolation.
Bulkowski discusses realistic expectation-setting given the failure rates documented throughout the book — since even his best-performing patterns fail a meaningful share of the time, money management and consistent risk control matter as much as pattern selection itself for long-term trading results.
The book closes by reiterating its central thesis across all pattern types: chart patterns are probabilistic tools that should be evaluated and traded based on actual measured statistics, not folklore-level assumptions about how reliably they "always" work.
keyLessons: Position sizing and pattern-specific stop-loss placement matter as much as which pattern you trade.
Combining multiple confirming signals reduces reliance on any single imperfect pattern.
Long-term results depend on disciplined risk management given known, non-zero pattern failure rates.
Treat chart patterns as probabilistic tools with measurable, non-zero failure rates, not guarantees.
Learn precise, consistent identification rules for a pattern before trusting its associated statistics.
Check whether a specific pattern variation (depth, volume behavior, trend context) correlates with stronger performance before trading it.
Distinguish reversal patterns from continuation patterns and match your trade thesis to the correct type.
Be skeptical of a pattern's popular reputation until you've checked its measured, statistical performance.
Use short-term patterns as one confirming input, not a standalone trade trigger.
Apply consistent position sizing and pattern-specific stop-loss placement across every trade.
Combine multiple confirming signals rather than relying on a single pattern in isolation.

conceptsFrameworks.name: Confirmation and Breakout
conceptsFrameworks.definition: Bulkowski's framework for when a chart pattern is considered statistically "activated" — typically the point at which price closes beyond a defined trendline or boundary of the pattern — which is the reference point from which his performance statistics (average rise/decline, failure rate) are measured.

conceptsFrameworks.name: Pattern Failure Rate
conceptsFrameworks.definition: The measured percentage of instances in which a given confirmed chart pattern does not perform as expected (for example, price fails to reach a minimum target move), used throughout the book as the primary quantitative check against a pattern's popular reputation.

conceptsFrameworks.name: Throwback and Pullback
conceptsFrameworks.definition: The tendency, measured pattern by pattern, for price to briefly retrace back to the pattern's breakout boundary after an initial breakout move before resuming in the breakout direction; Bulkowski measures how frequently this occurs and what it implies for entry timing.

actionSteps: Pick one chart pattern you currently trade and look up its specific, disclosed identification rules rather than relying on visual intuition, then re-check your last several trades against that precise definition.
Before your next pattern-based trade, note the measured failure rate for that specific pattern and size your position with that number explicitly in mind rather than assuming near-certainty.
Track throwback/pullback behavior on your next five pattern trades to see whether waiting for a retest changes your entry timing and results.
Choose one commonly-taught short-term pattern you currently trust and compare its popular reputation against measured statistical performance before continuing to rely on it as a standalone signal.
reflectionQuestions: Are you currently trading chart patterns based on their popular reputation or based on actual measured statistics for that specific pattern?
How would your position sizing change if you explicitly accounted for a pattern's real, non-zero historical failure rate?

points: Bulkowski's statistics are drawn from historical U.S. equity price data he personally compiled, so results may not generalize cleanly to other asset classes, markets, or trading regimes (different volatility environments, different market structures) without independent verification.

As with any backward-looking statistical study of chart patterns, there's an inherent risk that patterns which "worked" historically in his sample may perform differently going forward if enough traders act on the same documented statistics, altering the market behavior the statistics were based on.

The encyclopedia format, while extremely useful as a reference, does not build toward a single overarching trading system; readers looking for a complete, ready-to-use strategy rather than a statistical reference will need to construct that system themselves from the individual pattern data.

Technical/chart-pattern analysis as a discipline remains contested within mainstream academic finance, which is generally skeptical (per efficient-market-hypothesis-adjacent research) that historical price patterns reliably predict future price moves; Bulkowski's book operates within the practitioner technical-analysis tradition rather than engaging deeply with that academic debate.
criticalTake.contextNote: Bulkowski has continued to publish updated pattern research and statistics through his own website and later books, and treats his own historical statistics as subject to periodic revision as more data accumulates, rather than as fixed, final numbers.

whoThisIsFor: Active technical traders and chart pattern practitioners who want statistically grounded pattern data as a reference, rather than a beginner's introduction to trading or a single unified strategy.
whenToReadThis: Best used as an ongoing reference to consult pattern-by-pattern before specific trades, rather than read cover to cover in one sitting.

authorBio.name: Thomas N. Bulkowski
authorBio.bio:
Thomas Bulkowski is a self-taught, independent trader and technical analysis researcher based in Texas, known for building his own extensive personal database of chart pattern occurrences drawn from decades of historical stock price data, which forms the statistical backbone of his books.

He built his trading and research career independently, outside of a traditional Wall Street or academic finance path, and is widely regarded within retail and practitioner technical-analysis circles as one of the most statistically rigorous chart-pattern researchers publishing for a general trading audience.

Bulkowski has expanded his chart-pattern research across multiple books and maintains an active personal website where he continues to publish updated pattern statistics, reflecting an ongoing rather than one-time research effort.
